analysis.one_liner: Raises corporate tax rates on companies whose CEOs make far more than typical workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: the Ways and Means Committee took no action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a tax penalty on corporations where the CEO or highest-paid employee earns many times what the median worker makes. Companies whose pay ratio tops 50-to-1 would see their corporate tax rate rise, with the surcharge growing as the gap widens — up to 5 extra percentage points above the 21% corporate rate for ratios over 500-to-1. It applies only to large companies, exempts smaller private firms with less than $100 million in average annual gross receipts, and directs the Treasury to write rules preventing companies from gaming the ratio by swapping employees for contractors.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who would receive extra revenue from the most unequal large corporations, and workers at those companies, who would benefit if the tax pressure pushed their employers toward smaller CEO-to-worker pay gaps or more broadly shared raises. The bill does not directly pay any money to individuals; its benefit is a change in corporate incentives.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and workers at large unequal-pay firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the 21% corporate income tax rate by 0.5 to 5 percentage points depending on how far the CEO-to-median-worker pay ratio exceeds 50-to-1, reaching a 5-point increase for ratios over 500-to-1 [S2][S3].

It applies to corporations whose pay ratio exceeds 50 to 1, and uses the pay-ratio disclosure method that public companies already must report under SEC rules, extending the requirement to large private corporations with average annual gross receipts of at least $100 million [S2][S3].
The bill requires Treasury regulations to prevent companies from avoiding the penalty by changing workforce composition, including replacing employees with contractors [S3].
Corporations with average annual gross receipts under $100 million are exempt, so smaller businesses are not covered [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations with the biggest CEO-to-median-worker pay gaps would pay higher federal income tax — up to a 26% rate instead of 21%. Those costs could be borne by shareholders through lower profits, or partially passed to consumers and workers depending on the company. Companies could also avoid the tax by narrowing pay gaps.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporations with extreme CEO pay gaps

drawbacks.text: A tax on the pay ratio may not directly raise any worker's pay: a company could keep its pay structure and simply pay the higher tax, or restructure compensation in ways that shift costs to workers or contractors rather than narrowing the gap [S3].

The surcharge is relatively small — between 0.5 and 5 percentage points on a 21% rate — so for very profitable companies it may be a modest cost rather than a strong incentive to change pay practices [S2][S3].

Measuring median worker compensation across complex multinational workforces is difficult, and the bill relies on new Treasury regulations to make the ratio hard to manipulate, which creates administrative and compliance costs and potential disputes [S3].

The tax would raise revenue only from a subset of corporations, so it is a narrow, targeted levy rather than broad-based tax reform; businesses could also reduce reported median pay by shifting to contractors if the anti-avoidance rules fall short [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a modest, targeted tax rather than a pay mandate. Its strength is that it costs nothing for companies with reasonably tight pay gaps and puts a growing price tag on the most extreme ones, while explicitly trying to close the contractor loophole. Its limits are real: the surcharge is small enough that some companies would simply pay it, and nothing in the bill guarantees any worker a raise. Whether it changes behavior depends on how much executives value shareholder returns versus minimizing headline pay ratios.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it before the congressional session ended, so it died without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Barbara Lee of California introduced the Tax Excessive CEO Pay Act of 2024 in the House on January 18, 2024 [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day; that was the only action recorded in its history [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations with the widest CEO-to-worker pay gaps — and the wealthy executives they pay — came out ahead, because the tax penalty they would have faced was never enacted. No one else gained anything concrete from the bill's failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big corporations with huge CEO pay gaps

for.name: Rep. Barbara Lee

for.name: 13 Democratic House cosponsors
for.role: Original cosponsors including Tlaib, Norton, Watson Coleman, Khanna, Jayapal, and others
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors when the bill was introduced, with 15 total cosponsors by the end

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 18, 2024 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All 16 supporters (sponsor plus 15 cosponsors) were Democrats, and the committee that buried the bill was controlled by Republicans, so the bill followed a partisan pattern typical of Democratic tax proposals in a divided Congress [S3][S4][S5].

industries.industry: Large corporations with high CEO-to-worker pay ratios
industries.note: These companies would pay a higher federal tax rate — up to 5 points more than 21% — unless they narrow their internal pay gaps. Some could pass costs to shareholders, consumers, or workers, but the tax is designed to pressure them toward more equal pay.

Firms that design executive pay packages would face new pressure to justify or restructure compensation to avoid crossing ratio thresholds. Compliance and restructuring work could actually create demand for their services.
